To find the third-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!} \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to compute $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{x} & ⟹ &  & f(0) & ={e}^{0}=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={e}^{x} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & ={e}^{0}=1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={e}^{x} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & ={e}^{0}=1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & ={e}^{x} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(0) & ={e}^{0}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0)$ into our third-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =1+1\cdot x+1\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+1\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =1+x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
